terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where a few requests go to the old server and to your router.

tasks.title: Keep a table of routes
tasks.description:
Implement `createRouter()`, `addRoute(router, method, path, handler)` and the first part of `handle(router, req, res)` in `src/router.js`.

- `createRouter()` returns a new router with no routes; two routers never share their routes
- `addRoute` keeps a route: a method such as `'GET'`, a path such as `'/orders/today'`, and the handler for them
- it throws a `TypeError` when `path` is not a string that starts with `/`, or `handler` is not a function, and an `Error` when the router already has a route for that method and path
- `handle` calls the handler of the route whose method and path are exactly `req.method` and `req.url`, with the very `req` and `res` it was given, and no other handler

The check makes its own routers and routes, sends them requests of its own and notes which handlers ran.
nextSteps: Run `node src/try.js` and read the error.
Decide what a router holds, and return a fresh one from `createRouter()`.
In `addRoute`, check the path and the handler, then keep the route inside that router.
In `handle`, look for the route with the request's method and path, and call its handler.
hints: A router is only data: a list of routes, or an object of paths. What matters is that each call to `createRouter()` makes a new one.
A route is the method and the path together. Two routes may share a path when their methods differ, and that is the only time they may.
`router.routes.find((route) => route.method === req.method && route.path === req.url)` finds the route. Call `route.handler(req, res)` when there is one.

tasks.title: Say when there is no route
tasks.description:
Make `handle` answer a request whose path has no route at all, under any method.

- the answer is status `404`, sent with `sendJson`
- its body is `{ error }`, a sentence that names the method and the path of the request, such as `There is no route for GET /invoices.`
- no handler runs
- a path matches a route only when it is exactly the route's path, letter for letter: `/orders/1873` is not `/orders`, and `/Orders` is not `/orders`

The check sends requests for paths its routes do not have, some close to ones they do, and reads the answer.
nextSteps: Run `node src/try.js`: look at what your router does with `/orders/todays-list` and `/Prices`.
Find every route with the request's path, whatever its method.
When there are none, answer 404 with `sendJson` and say which request it was.
hints: The old server matched with `startsWith`, which is why `/orders/todays-list` got today's orders. A path is the same path only when every character is the same.
Answering is what a handler would do: set the status, set the content type, end the response. `sendJson(res, status, value)` does all three.
``sendJson(res, 404, { error: `There is no route for ${req.method} ${req.url}.` })`` is the whole answer.

tasks.title: Say which methods a path takes
tasks.description:
Make `handle` answer a request whose path has routes, but none for its method.

- the answer is status `405`, sent with `sendJson`
- it has an `allow` header that lists the methods of this path's routes, in the order they were added, separated by a comma and a space: `GET, POST`
- its body is `{ error }`, a sentence that names the method and the path of the request
- no handler runs, the one for another method included

The check sends requests with methods its paths do not take and reads the status, the `allow` header and the body.
nextSteps: You already found the routes with this path. Which methods do they have?
Set the `allow` header before `sendJson` ends the response, then answer 405.
hints: A 404 says there is nothing here. A 405 says there is something here, just not for this method, and the `allow` header says what would work.
Headers go out before the body, so set them before the response ends: `res.setHeader(name, value)` after `res.end()` throws.
